subject: web-technology-2
name: Web Technology II
exam: TU assessment: 60% final examination set by the university, 40% internal (assignments, lab work, attendance). Confirm the split in your college's notice.

units.title: Server-Side Scripting and PHP Fundamentals
topics: Including files and running from the command line
Seeing the ideas: from request to running PHP

sections.title: Including files and running from the command line
Seeing the ideas: from request to running PHP

summary: PHP runs on the server, generates HTML dynamically and can reach files and databases; the browser never sees the source.
The language is loosely typed, with strict mode and type declarations available; use ===.
Arrays are the universal data structure; functions can take defaults, references, variadics and named arguments.
Files are shared with include/require; the command line and the built-in server make testing easy.

units.title: Forms, Files, Sessions and Cookies
topics: Seeing the ideas: how data travels between browser and server

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: how data travels between browser and server

summary: Form data arrives in GET and _POST; it must be validated and escaped because it comes from an untrusted user.
PHP reads and writes files and CSV, handles dates and uploads, but each of these needs defensive checks.
Cookies keep small data in the browser; sessions keep state on the server and identify the user with a random ID.

units.title: MySQL for Web Applications
topics: Aggregate functions, GROUP BY and HAVING
Seeing the ideas: how MySQL stores, filters and joins data

sections.title: Aggregate functions, GROUP BY and HAVING
Seeing the ideas: how MySQL stores, filters and joins data

summary: MySQL stores web data in tables; types, keys and constraints describe and protect it.
A handful of statements (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) with WHERE, grouping, subqueries and joins covers most web needs.
The server enforces constraints with clear errors, so design them into the schema.

units.title: Connecting PHP to MySQL
topics: Prepared statements: the only safe way
Seeing the ideas: PHP talking to MySQL

sections.title: Prepared statements: the only safe way
Seeing the ideas: PHP talking to MySQL

summary: PHP talks to MySQL through mysqli or PDO: connect, query, fetch, close, with exceptions for errors.
Prepared statements separate SQL from data and are the defence against SQL injection.
CRUD, pagination and transactions are small patterns repeated across every web application.

units.title: Object-Oriented Programming in PHP
topics: Static members, constants and class methods
Seeing the ideas: classes, objects and contracts

sections.title: Static members, constants and class methods
Seeing the ideas: classes, objects and contracts

summary: PHP objects bundle state and behaviour, with constructor promotion and visibility modifiers for encapsulation.
Inheritance, abstract classes and interfaces give polymorphism and contracts; traits reuse code.
Static members and the singleton pattern share state; exceptions make errors explicit.

units.title: AJAX, JSON and Web APIs
topics: A PHP endpoint and a real HTTP request
Seeing the ideas: AJAX, JSON and REST

sections.title: A PHP endpoint and a real HTTP request
Seeing the ideas: AJAX, JSON and REST

summary: AJAX updates part of a page using a background request; JSON is the usual data format.
A PHP endpoint decodes input, validates it, uses prepared statements, and returns JSON with correct headers and status codes.
The browser side uses fetch or XMLHttpRequest (or jQuery); output inserted into the page must be escaped.

units.title: Web Application Security and Authentication
topics: A complete registration and login flow
Seeing the ideas: attacks, defences and the three factors

sections.title: A complete registration and login flow
Seeing the ideas: attacks, defences and the three factors

summary: Injection, XSS and CSRF all come from trusting input; each has a standard defence.
Passwords are stored as slow salted hashes; the login flow regenerates the session ID and reveals nothing about which part failed.
Security is a checklist applied to every form, query and output, not a feature added at the end.

units.title: Content Management Systems and PHP Frameworks
topics: Seeing the ideas: CMS layers, MVC, hooks, autoloading and deployment

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: CMS layers, MVC, hooks, autoloading and deployment

summary: A CMS lets non-programmers manage content; WordPress and Joomla differ in structure but share themes/templates, plugins/extensions and an admin panel on PHP and MySQL.
MVC structures applications into model, view, controller and router; frameworks like Laravel provide the plumbing.
Deployment adds HTTPS, secure configuration and backups.
